chapter_theme: The fine points of sulking, a comedy of jealous logic. Every word he says, every sneeze, whether he hides it or not, whether he pleads or looks, is turned into evidence. It is the most purely entertaining chapter in the Kural, and it also shows how love trains two people in close reading.
structure_note: The woman speaks in 1311-1312. The man speaks in 1313-1320, telling her friend about it on Parimelazhagar's reading, with the woman's words quoted in each verse. The chapter's last line in several verses is what she said.

1311.reading: The woman calls him a philanderer and refuses his chest, because all women feast on him in common with their eyes.
1311.nuance: The offence is only that he was seen, and being seen is a form of being consumed. பரத்த is applied to him in the vocative, and is the verse's own word for his straying.

positions.position: பெண்ணியலார் means courtesans, who, lacking other virtues, have only the nature of women. They look at him as his procession passes.
positions.quote: பரத்தையர்க்குள்ளது பெண் இயற்கை மாத்திரமே என்னுங் கருத்தால், 'பெண் இயலார்' என்றாள்.

positions.position: It simply means all women, who think of his chest as common property.
positions.quote: நின் மார்பைப் பெண்மை யுடையா ரெல்லாரும் தமக்குப் பொதுவாக நினைத்துக்

1312.reading: The woman tells her friend that while she was sulking he sneezed, knowing she would then say 'long life' and so break her silence.
1312.nuance: A real gem of observed domestic strategy. Parimelazhagar says what makes this a 'fine point': she takes a natural sneeze for a deliberate sign. We can't tell if he meant it, and that is the fun.

1313.reading: The man tells her friend that even if he wears a wreath of bent flowers, she is angry and says he wore it to show some other woman.
1313.nuance: The word கோட்டுப்பூ is a puzzle. Parimelazhagar offers flowers woven in a curve or flowers from another landscape, Manakkudavar offers side-worn flowers, and Kalaignar flowers from a tree-branch. The offence doesn't depend on the answer, which is the point.

1314.reading: The man says he told her he loved more than anyone, and she sulked: 'than whom, than whom?'
1314.nuance: A grammatical quarrel. He meant 'we love more than any other couple', and she took it to mean 'more than the other women I love'. The commentators spell this out, and the verse gives only her repeated words, one of the most natural bits of speech in the book.

1315.reading: The man says he told her they wouldn't part in this birth, and her eyes filled with tears.
1315.nuance: A promise made in the language of rebirth backfires on its own qualifier: 'in this birth' implies 'not in the next'. Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar explain it so. Kalaignar has her ask 'is there a next birth, then?', which is a modern touch that isn't in the verse. Rebirth is taken for granted, as material for a joke.

1316.reading: The man says he told her he had thought of her, and she said 'why did you forget?', and wouldn't embrace him, and went into a sulk.
1316.nuance: A strict logical inference, and Parimelazhagar uses a term from Indian logic for it, அருத்தாபத்தி: remembering presupposes forgetting. She is using the man's own argument from 1125.

1317.reading: The man says that when he sneezed she blessed him, and then undid it and wept: 'who were you thinking of, that you sneezed?'
1317.nuance: The blessing comes automatically and the suspicion comes a second later, and the verse catches that interval. Parimelazhagar notes that the belief behind this is a women's usage (மகளிர் வழக்கு) and that she's taking it as literal fact.

1318.reading: The man says that when he suppressed a sneeze, she wept: 'are you hiding from me that your people are thinking of you?'
1318.nuance: It's the next stage of the farce. He has learned from 1317, and that's now the crime. Parimelazhagar sums it up: it's a fault to sneeze and a fault not to. So what is there to do?

1319.reading: The man says that even when he tries to appease her, she is angry and says that this is how he behaves with other women too.
1319.nuance: The cure has become evidence. Parimelazhagar notes the extra detail: he has even admitted to faults he didn't commit in order to placate her, and that confession is what now counts against him.

1320.reading: The man says that even when he just sits and gazes at her in thought, she is angry: 'whom are you thinking of as you look me over?'
1320.nuance: Silence and adoration are his last resort, and they fail too. For Parimelazhagar, her logic is very neat: as no one woman could match all her parts, he must be comparing each part with a different woman, so there must be several. So she wants them named.

links.note: The same folk belief at two points in the story. In 1203 she longs for a sneeze as proof he's thinking of her. In 1317 he sneezes in front of her, and the same belief proves someone else is thinking of him. A sign that means what one fears can't be falsified.

In 1125, the man is clever at the friend's expense: I would remember her if I forgot. 1316 shows the woman turning this logic on him: you say you remembered, so you forgot. His own wit has become the trap.

On Parimelazhagar's reading of 1262, she keeps him in mind at death so as to reach him in the next birth. In 1315, 'this birth' is what makes her cry. Rebirth, for the renunciant a fate to escape, is in this book something lovers want to share.

In 1113, he went over her body part by part, comparing it to shoots, pearls and spears, and she was pleased to be praised. In 1320 she treats that very habit of comparing part by part as evidence that he has others in mind. The praise of chapter 112 is the root of the suspicion.

source_issues: 1320: Manakkudavar's entry ends with கரியது, a typo for கூறியது.
1315, 1319: Parimelazhagar's notes have a character corruption, வௌ¢ப்படு and தௌ¢.
1311: Parimelazhagar's note has நுணக்கமாயிற்று, a typo for நுணுக்கமாயிற்று.
